chief_complaint: projectile, non-bilious vomiting immediately after every feeding in a 5-week-old male infant with olive mass (Pyloric Stenosis)
hpi_details: 5-week-old first-born male infant brought by parents due to 1-week history of progressively worsening vomiting. Initially regurgitated small amounts, but over the past 4 days has developed forceful, projectile vomiting immediately after every formula bottle feeding. Vomit shoots across the crib and consists purely of curdled milk without any green/yellow bile. Immediately after vomiting, the baby appears ravenously hungry and demands to feed again. Infant has had decreasing wet diapers and weight loss over the past week.
ideas: parents distressed watching baby forcefully projectile vomit all nourishment and lose weight
concerns: parents worried baby is starving and severely dehydrated
expectations: want immediate IV fluids and surgery to open up his stomach passage
pmh: First-born male infant, born at term without complications. Mother received oral Erythromycin during late pregnancy for bronchitis

clinical_knowledge.topic: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes CRITICAL RULE: Pyloric stenosis is a MEDICAL emergency first, NOT an immediate surgical emergency, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: projectile, non-bilious vomiting immediately after every feeding in a 5-week-old male infant with olive mass (Pyloric Stenosis)

Key HPI features: 5-week-old first-born male infant brought by parents due to 1-week history of progressively worsening vomiting. Initially regurgitated small amounts, but over the past 4 days has developed forceful, projectile vomiting immediately after every formula bottle feeding. Vomit shoots across the crib and consists purely of curdled milk without any green/yellow bile. Immediately after vomiting, the baby appears ravenously hungry and demands to feed again. Infant has had decreasing wet diapers and weight loss over the past week.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 162, RR 36, Temp 36.8C, Weight 3.6 kg (down 300g from birth weight). Infant appears dehydrated with depressed anterior fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, and loss of skin turgor. Abdominal palpation during feeding while the infant is quiet/sucking reveals a firm, 2 x 1.5 cm mobile, olive-shaped mass palpable in the right upper quadrant / epigastrium. Visible gastric peristaltic waves travel across the upper abdomen from left to right prior to emesis. Labs confirm hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis: pH 7.52, HCO3 32 mEq/L, Chloride 86 mEq/L, Potassium 3.1 mEq/L. Abdominal ultrasound confirms Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis: pyloric muscle thickness 4.8 mm (diagnostic >3-4 mm) and pyloric channel length 19 mm (diagnostic >14-16 mm).
Relevant background/PMH: First-born male infant, born at term without complications. Mother received oral Erythromycin during late pregnancy for bronchitis
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Gastroesophageal reflux without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Projectile non-bilious vomiting.
management_principles: CRITICAL RULE: Pyloric stenosis is a MEDICAL emergency first, NOT an immediate surgical emergency
NPO immediately and place nasogastric tube to decompression

Correct dehydration and electrolyte imbalance before surgery with isotonic IV fluid; add dextrose and potassium only after adequate urine output, and recheck electrolytes and acid-base status before anesthesia
Proceed to pyloromyotomy only after adequate resuscitation and correction of clinically significant alkalosis and electrolyte abnormalities
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 5-week-old first-born male presenting with progressive, forceful non-bilious projectile vomiting, ravenous hunger post-emesis, and failure to thrive.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 162, RR 36, Temp 36.8C, Weight 3.6 kg (down 300g from birth weight). Infant appears dehydrated with depressed anterior fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, and loss of skin turgor. Abdominal palpation during feeding while the infant is quiet/sucking reveals a firm, 2 x 1.5 cm mobile, olive-shaped mass palpable in the right upper quadrant / epigastrium. Visible gastric peristaltic waves travel across the upper abdomen from left to right prior to emesis. Labs confirm hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis: pH 7.52, HCO3 32 mEq/L, Chloride 86 mEq/L, Potassium 3.1 mEq/L. Abdominal ultrasound confirms Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis: pyloric muscle thickness 4.8 mm (diagnostic >3-4 mm) and pyloric channel length 19 mm (diagnostic >14-16 mm).
reference_soap.assessment: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis complicated by severe Hypochloremic Hypokalemic Metabolic Alkalosis and dehydration.
reference_soap.plan: Pyloric stenosis requires medical stabilization before, rather than immediate, surgery. 1. Keep the infant NPO; use gastric decompression if clinically indicated. 2. Correct dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities with isotonic IV fluid; add dextrose and potassium only after urine output is established, with serial electrolyte and acid-base reassessment. 3. Once adequately resuscitated and metabolically stable for anesthesia, proceed to laparoscopic or open Ramstedt extramucosal pyloromyotomy.

learning_objectives: Identify clinical hallmarks of Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (3-8 week old male, non-bilious projectile vomiting, ravenous hunger post-emesis, palpable olive-shaped epigastric mass)
Explain the pathophysiology of hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis secondary to persistent loss of gastric hydrochloric acid and renal potassium wasting
Understand the critical mandate that preoperative correction of metabolic alkalosis and electrolyte deficits takes absolute priority over surgical intervention before general anesthesia
Interpret abdominal ultrasound diagnostic criteria (pyloric muscle thickness >3-4 mm, channel length >14-16 mm) and outline Ramstedt pyloromyotomy technique

teaching.one_liner: 5-week-old first-born male with progressive non-bilious projectile vomiting after every feed, ravenous hunger after vomiting, and weight loss.
differentials: Malrotation with volvulus (bilious vomiting would suggest this)
red_flags: Weight loss and decreased wet diapers

must_ask.objective: Characterize the vomiting as projectile and non-bilious
must_ask.say: Does the vomit shoot out forcefully, and is it just milk without any green or yellow color?
Does he seem very hungry and want to feed again right after vomiting?

must_ask.objective: Assess hydration status through wet diapers
must_ask.say: How many wet diapers is he having per day compared to before?

must_ask.objective: Track the timeline of symptom progression
must_ask.say: When did the vomiting start, and has it gotten worse over the past week?

must_ask.objective: Explain that fluid correction comes before surgery
must_ask.say: Before any surgery, we first need to correct his fluids and electrolytes with an IV — this comes first, even though he'll need an operation eventually.

history.answer: Our five-week-old baby boy shoots up his milk forcefully every time we feed him.
He started spitting up small amounts a week ago, but over the last four days it has gotten much worse and turns into forceful vomiting after every bottle.
He vomits immediately after every single bottle feed, right as he finishes drinking.
It is curdled white formula milk that smells sour, without any blood or dark specks.
No, there is definitely no green or yellowish bile in what he brings up.
Yes, it shoots several feet across his crib like a projectile, not like gentle reflux or normal spitting up.
Right after he throws up, he acts ravenously hungry and screams desperately to be fed again.
He does not seem to have belly cramps between feedings, but he fusses right before vomiting and then calms down immediately.
He still passes gas, but his stools have become very small, hard, and infrequent over the past few days.
No, he has had no fever at all, and no one else at home has been sick.
He has become noticeably more lethargic and sleepy today compared to his usual self.
No, he has had no falls, bumps to the head, or any injuries.
His diapers have been almost dry; he used to have six or seven wet diapers a day, but today he only had one small wet diaper.
His mouth and lips look very dry, and when he cries, he barely produces any tears.
Yes, he was three point nine kilograms at birth and the clinic scale showed he dropped down to three point six kilograms today.
He takes about three to four ounces of standard cow milk formula every three hours, but he throws all of it right back up.
No, he has had no cough, wheezing, or difficulty breathing.
We are terrified that he is starving and severely dehydrated, and we hope you can give him IV fluids and perform surgery to open his stomach.
He has had no medical illnesses or health issues since birth.
He has never had any operations or hospital stays.
He is not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter drops, or supplements.
He has no known allergies to medications or anything else.
He was born full-term at thirty-nine weeks by normal vaginal delivery without any complications.
His mother was prescribed oral erythromycin for severe bronchitis during her third trimester of pregnancy.
His vaccinations are completely up to date, including his Hepatitis B shots at birth and one month.
There is no family history of stomach problems, intestinal blockages, or childhood digestive disorders.
He lives at home with both of us in a smoke-free apartment, and neither of us smokes or drinks.
He stays at home under our care and has not been exposed to daycare or anyone who is sick.

exam.finding: Lethargic, ill-appearing infant with a depressed anterior fontanelle, sunken eyes, and marked signs of dehydration.
Blood pressure 80/50 mmHg, heart rate 162/min, respiratory rate 36/min, body temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Dry oral mucosa, cracked lips, and absent tears during crying.
Decreased skin turgor with skin tenting on the abdomen and delayed capillary refill of 3 seconds.
Visible gastric peristaltic waves moving from left to right across the epigastrium prior to emesis; no surgical scars.
Normal bowel sounds heard throughout all four quadrants with no bruits.
Firm, mobile, olive-shaped mass measuring approximately 2 by 1.5 cm palpable in the right upper quadrant and epigastrium during calm bottle sucking, with no peritoneal tenderness.
Supple neck with full passive range of motion and no nuchal rigidity.
Current body weight is 3.6 kg, down 300 grams from his birth weight of 3.9 kg.
